strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical framework connecting diagonal loading, tightness of the continuous relaxation, and the maximum-clique-based Motzkin-Straus theorem. The extension (Theorem 4) and the extension of Barman's Lemma 5.1 (Theorem 2) are non-trivial and improve the known sufficient threshold for tightness from λ=2 to λ=1, with a matching lower bound (Corollary 2) showing this is essentially tight for the regime k<ω.

The landscape analysis (Lemma 1, Theorem 5) gives a clear, useful qualitative explanation for why larger λ hurts practical optimization (introduces spurious local maxima) even though it does not affect tightness, which nicely motivates the choice λ=1 used in the algorithms.

Two concrete, projection-free algorithms are proposed (Frank-Wolfe with a closed-form LMP, and a novel sigmoid/softmax-style parameterization generalizing to the Dkn polytope) together with careful per-iteration complexity analysis (O(m+k log n) for Frank-Wolfe).

Experiments span a good range of real graphs from ~4K to ~3M vertices and ~117M edges, which is considerably larger than what most baselines (L-ADMM, EXPP, LRBO) have been tested on, and the paper reports both density and runtime, showing the Frank-Wolfe variant is competitive or better while being much faster than L-ADMM/EXPP/AdamW-parameterization on large graphs.

The paper situates itself carefully with respect to a large body of prior DkS relaxation/approximation work and clearly explains the technical differences from related Frank-Wolfe-for-DSG works and from prior diagonal-loading papers.
weaknesses: The reference list includes [48] 'Q. Lu, N. D. Sidiropoulos, A. Konar, Densest k-subgraph mining via a provably tight relaxation, AAAI 2025,' whose title is essentially identical to the core theoretical claim of this manuscript (a 'provably tight' relaxation for DkS), yet this paper is never discussed, cited, or differentiated anywhere in the main text. Given the overlapping author affiliation with the cited Lovász-extension paper [39] (also co-authored by Sidiropoulos), this is a serious and unexplained gap: it is unclear whether the tightness result being presented here has already been established in [48], whether this submission is a substantially overlapping or duplicate contribution, or how the two works relate technically. This omission undermines the ability to assess the novelty of the central theoretical claim.

The tightness result (λ=1 is minimal) is rigorously shown to fail only in the specific regime k<ω via a simplex-relaxation counterexample; for k≥ω the paper explicitly states tightness at smaller λ 'may (but is not guaranteed to)' hold, so the claimed general minimality of λ=1 is not fully established for all k, weakening the generality of the headline result.

Frank-Wolfe convergence guarantees given are only to stationary points of the non-convex relaxed problem; despite the relaxation being provably tight at λ=1, there is no end-to-end approximation guarantee connecting the algorithm's output to the DkS optimum, so the practical benefit of the tightness theory is only indirectly supported by landscape heuristics and empirical results.

The experimental protocol appears to use a single run per (dataset, k) setting with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds/initializations, despite the objective being non-convex and the algorithms being sensitive to initialization and step-size choices (as shown in the λ and step-size ablations); this limits the statistical reliability of the density/runtime comparisons in Figures 4–5.

The parameterization/AdamW approach is motivated at length (Section 3.2, 3.3) but empirically underperforms Frank-Wolfe in most cases and is computationally much more expensive; the paper offers only speculative explanations ('may be related to the landscape', 'PyTorch matrix computations are costlier than NumPy') rather than a rigorous diagnosis, making the value of this second contribution unclear relative to the added complexity of presenting and analyzing it.

Baseline comparisons could be viewed as somewhat favorable to the proposed method: LRBO is restricted to rank-1 (rather than higher-rank) due to complexity concerns, and L-ADMM/EXPP show erratic runtime spikes (Figure 5) that are not explained, raising questions about whether these baselines were properly tuned or implemented under comparable conditions.

The gains in normalized edge density over the strongest baselines (L-ADMM, EXPP) are often modest, particularly at larger k or on harder graphs (e.g., soc-Pokec, web-Stanford), and the paper's narrative emphasizing Frank-Wolfe as a clear state-of-the-art winner is not uniformly supported by the figures.

strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical narrative: it tightens the known sufficient diagonal-loading threshold for exactness of the DkS relaxation from λ=2 (Barman) to λ=1, via a non-trivial extension of the Motzkin-Straus theorem and an extension of Barman's Lemma 5.1. The proofs in the appendices appear technically careful and self-contained.

Landscape analysis (Lemma 1, Theorem 5) offering monotonicity of local maxima as λ increases is a nice complement to the tightness result and gives some principled guidance (albeit imperfect, see weaknesses) for choosing λ.

Two projection-free algorithms (Frank-Wolfe and a sigmoid/softmax-style parameterization for the more general simplex-type constraint) are described with detailed per-iteration complexity analysis, and the FW variant scales to graphs with millions of vertices/tens of millions of edges, which is practically valuable.

The experimental comparison spans six real datasets across a range of subgraph sizes and includes a reasonably comprehensive baseline set (Greedy, LRBO, L-ADMM, EXPP) plus a meaningful upper bound reference curve.
weaknesses: Reference [48] 'Densest k-subgraph mining via a provably tight relaxation' (Lu, Sidiropoulos, Konar, AAAI 2025) is listed in the bibliography but is never discussed, cited in-line, or compared against anywhere in the paper, despite having an almost identical title and thesis to this submission's central claim ('provably tight relaxation' for DkS). This is a serious and unexplained omission: it is unclear whether this prior work already establishes similar or stronger tightness results and/or algorithms, and without discussion the paper's novelty and significance relative to the state of the art cannot be properly assessed. This alone raises serious concerns about the originality of the central contribution.

The claim that λ=1 is 'the minimum value of λ to ensure the relaxation is tight for general k' is not actually established for general k. Corollary 2's tightness-failure argument is proven only in the regime k<ω (subgraph size smaller than the clique number); for k≥ω, the paper explicitly states the relaxation 'may (but is not guaranteed to) be tight' for λ<1. The generalization implied in the surrounding text (and in the abstract/contributions) is thus overstated relative to what is rigorously proven.

There is a tension between the theoretical recommendation and its practical implementation: Lemma 1 (no spurious non-integral local maxima) only holds for λ>1 strictly, not at the recommended λ=1. Consequently, at the chosen operating point λ=1, non-integral local optima can and do occur, which is why the algorithms still require an ad hoc projection/post-processing step onto B^n_k, identical to what the baselines (L-ADMM, EXPP) already require. This undercuts the practical payoff of the tightness result, since the tightness guarantee (for global optima) does not translate into a benign landscape for the local, gradient-based algorithms actually used.

The λ-selection experiments (Figures 2-3) are conducted on a single, small dataset (Facebook, n=4039) with a single k, and the resulting choice (λ=1, Option I step size) is then applied uniformly to all other datasets without further empirical validation that this choice remains near-optimal at larger scale or different graph structures.

In several of the larger/sparser graphs (soc-Pokec, as-Skitter, web-Stanford), the density plots show the proposed FW method is not clearly dominant and is sometimes matched or exceeded by L-ADMM/EXPP, weakening the claim that FW 'stands out' broadly; the improvement margins in these cases are fairly narrow and no statistical variability (e.g., over multiple runs/seeds, tie-breaking in top-k) is reported.

The two proposed algorithmic ideas (Frank-Wolfe for a linearly-constrained non-convex QP, and a sigmoid/softmax reparameterization for box+ (in)equality constraints) are largely applications of well-established techniques rather than substantial methodological innovations; the complexity analysis is thorough but the algorithmic novelty is modest.

The paper does not report confidence intervals, variance, or sensitivity to the arbitrary tie-breaking in top_k(x), nor does it discuss how robust the reported density/time numbers are to random initialization or floating-point tie-breaking, which is relevant given the non-convex optimization landscape being emphasized throughout the paper.

strengths: Clean and non-trivial theoretical contribution: the paper tightens the previously known sufficient diagonal-loading threshold for exact relaxation tightness from λ=2 (Barman) to λ=1, and shows via an extension of the Motzkin-Straus theorem that λ=1 is also necessary in a specific regime (k<ω), giving a matching lower/upper bound argument that is more refined than prior work.

Landscape analysis (Lemma 1, Theorem 5) is a nice complement to the tightness result: it shows that increasing λ beyond 1 can only introduce (not remove) spurious local maxima, giving a principled justification (rather than purely empirical tuning as in prior works [35],[37],[41]) for choosing λ=1 in practice.

Two complementary projection-free algorithms are proposed (Frank-Wolfe and a novel sigmoid/temperature-based parameterization of the more general Dn_k constraint), each with an explicit per-iteration complexity analysis, which is a useful practical contribution for scaling to large graphs.

Fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across six real graphs spanning several orders of magnitude in size (up to ~3M vertices / 117M edges), with multiple relevant baselines (Greedy, LRBO, L-ADMM, EXPP) and an informative theoretical upper bound for context, plus ablations on λ and Frank-Wolfe step-size choices that are consistent with the theory.

The Frank-Wolfe method is shown to be both accurate (near the density upper bound in several cases) and computationally cheap relative to baselines of comparable quality, supporting the paper's central practical claim about scalability.
weaknesses: Reference [48] ("Densest k-subgraph mining via a provably tight relaxation," AAAI 2025, authored by names that overlap with likely authors/collaborators of this manuscript, e.g., Sidiropoulos, Konar) is listed in the bibliography but never discussed, cited, or differentiated from in the main text, despite its title suggesting extremely close overlap with this paper's central claim (a "provably tight relaxation" for DkS). This is a serious omission: readers cannot assess how the present paper's tightness result, algorithms, or experiments relate to or improve upon this apparently very closely related (possibly prior) work by the same or overlapping authors, raising concerns about the paper's claimed novelty and self-citation practices.

The practical relevance of the tightness result is somewhat indirect: Corollary 1/Theorem 2 guarantee that a *global* maximizer of the relaxation is integral for λ≥1, but the proposed algorithms (Frank-Wolfe, AdamW on the parameterization) are only guaranteed to converge to stationary points/local maxima of a non-convex problem, so the connection between the tightness theorem and the empirically observed benefits of λ=1 is established only qualitatively (via Theorem 5) rather than with a rigorous guarantee tying local-search outcomes to solution quality.

Corollary 2's proof of the λ=1 lower bound is restricted to the regime k<ω, yet the surrounding discussion states more broadly that λ=1 is "the minimum value of λ to ensure that the relaxation is tight for general k," which somewhat overstates what was proven; the authors do note this caveat but the phrasing is potentially misleading.

Experimental protocol details raise reproducibility/robustness concerns: results appear to be based on single runs (no repeated trials, variance, or confidence intervals reported) despite AdamW and Frank-Wolfe being sensitive to initialization/step-size choices; a fixed iteration budget (200) is used uniformly across graphs differing by orders of magnitude in size, which could unfairly penalize or advantage certain methods/datasets and makes head-to-head runtime/density comparisons harder to interpret.

The parameterization/AdamW approach is shown to have O(n^2) per-iteration cost in one regime, which is markedly worse than the Frank-Wolfe algorithm's O(m + k log n); given this, its inclusion as a primary proposed method for very large graphs (e.g., com-Orkut with n≈3M) seems questionable, and its comparatively weak empirical performance somewhat undercuts the paper's claim that it is a competitive standalone contribution rather than largely a secondary/ablation method.

The problem setting (DkS) is fairly specialized within combinatorial/graph optimization; while the theoretical and algorithmic contributions are solid, the significance and broader ML relevance of the specific incremental improvement (λ=2→λ=1 tightness threshold) may be viewed as narrow relative to ICML's general audience, absent a clearer articulation of downstream impact beyond graph-mining benchmarks.

strengths: Sharpens a known result: extends Barman's Lemma 5.1 to show λ=1 (rather than λ=2) suffices for tightness of the diagonal-loaded relaxation, and complements this with a novel extension of the Motzkin–Straus theorem to establish a matching lower bound, giving a clean, essentially tight characterization of the minimal diagonal loading parameter.

Provides landscape analysis (Lemma 1, Theorem 5) showing that increasing λ beyond the tightness threshold can only introduce (not remove) spurious local maxima, giving a principled justification for using the minimal λ=1 rather than the more conservative PSD-based λ used in classical convex maximization results.

Proposes two projection-free algorithms (Frank–Wolfe and an explicit sigmoid/softmax-style constraint parameterization for the more general Dⁿ_k set) with detailed per-iteration complexity analysis, addressing a genuine scalability bottleneck of prior SDP/ADMM/LP-based DkS relaxations.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across six real-world graphs spanning several orders of magnitude in size (up to ~3M nodes, ~117M edges) against multiple relevant baselines (Greedy, LRBO, L-ADMM, EXPP) with both density and runtime comparisons.

Clear exposition of the relationships between the various problem reformulations/relaxations (Figure 1) and a well-organized related-work discussion that accurately situates the contribution relative to prior diagonal-loading and relaxation-based DkS work.
weaknesses: The ablation studies motivating the choice λ=1 and the Frank–Wolfe step-size option (Section 4.4, 4.5) are conducted only on the smallest dataset (Facebook), leaving it unclear whether these qualitative landscape/convergence observations generalize to the larger, sparser graphs used in the main comparison.

The lower-bound argument in Corollary 2 establishing that λ<1 cannot guarantee tightness relies on a specific regime (k<ω, uniform-clique-type solutions) rather than a fully general adversarial construction across all k, so the claim that λ=1 is 'the' minimum value for general k, while plausible, is argued somewhat narrowly.

No statistical robustness reporting (e.g., variance across multiple runs/initializations, random seeds) is provided for the experiments, despite the algorithms being randomized/iterative and results (Figures 4–5) showing fairly noisy density/runtime curves.

The second proposed algorithm (parameterization + AdamW) is shown to be generally inferior to Frank–Wolfe in both density and runtime, and its O(n^2) per-iteration cost in one branch undermines the scalability motivation; its inclusion as a core contribution is only weakly justified empirically.

Comparisons omit exact or near-optimal small-scale baselines (e.g., ILP/SDP solutions on the smallest graph) that could quantify the actual optimality gap rather than relying solely on a loose spectral upper bound, which is often far from tight (visible in several panels of Figure 4).

The theoretical results are specific to unweighted, simple graphs; it is not discussed whether/how the tightness and landscape results extend to weighted graphs, which are common in the motivating applications (e.g., financial transaction networks) mentioned in the introduction.

strengths: The paper improves upon a known tightness result for diagonally-loaded DkS relaxations (Barman's λ=2 bound) by deriving a tighter sufficient bound (λ≥1) via a non-trivial extension of the Motzkin–Straus theorem and an extension of a lemma from prior work, providing a matching upper and lower bound argument for the studied parameter regime.

The landscape analysis (Lemma 1, Theorem 5) offering monotonicity of local maxima with respect to λ is a nice theoretical complement that helps explain empirically observed phenomena (larger λ trapping the optimizer in spurious local maxima).

Two practical, projection-free algorithms (Frank–Wolfe and an explicit sigmoid/softmax-style reparameterization for the Dn_k polytope) are proposed with detailed per-iteration complexity analysis; the FW variant scales to graphs with millions of vertices and tens of millions of edges.
Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across 6 real datasets of varying scale against multiple relevant baselines (Greedy, LRBO, L-ADMM, EXPP) as well as a theoretical upper bound on density.
The parameterization for the general cardinality constraint set (not just the k=1 simplex/softmax case) appears to be a novel technical device that could be reused elsewhere.
weaknesses: The central tightness claim is oversold relative to what is actually proven: Corollary 2's proof only establishes non-tightness for λ<1 in the specific regime k<ω (where the extended Motzkin–Straus result is exploited); the text explicitly concedes that for other k the relaxation "may (but is not guaranteed to) be tight" for λ<1, yet the paper still states without qualification that "λ=1 is the minimum value of λ to ensure that the relaxation is tight for general k." This is an important precision problem in the paper's main theoretical claim.

The theoretical machinery (extension of a Caratheodory-type rounding lemma and of Motzkin–Straus) is somewhat incremental: the underlying proof techniques (swap arguments, induction over vertex removal) closely mirror existing arguments in the cited works, and the resulting improvement (λ=2→λ=1) is useful but modest in scope.

The experimental section lacks statistical rigor: parameter/step-size sensitivity (Figures 2–3) is demonstrated on a single small dataset (Facebook) only, with no repeated trials, confidence intervals, or sensitivity analysis on larger/sparser graphs where the clique-size assumptions underlying the theory may behave differently.

The empirical superiority of the Frank–Wolfe method is not consistent across all datasets/subgraph sizes (e.g., in web-Stanford, com-Youtube, soc-Pokec, com-Orkut plots, Param-AdamW or other baselines are sometimes comparable or better), yet the abstract/contributions claim "state-of-the-art" performance somewhat broadly; the qualifying language in the text ("generally," "in the vast majority of cases") is not well quantified (e.g., no aggregate win-rate or statistical summary across settings).

No explicit Limitations section; scalability/validity boundaries of the theory (e.g., what happens when k is close to or exceeds ω, or for weighted/directed graphs excluded by preprocessing) are not discussed.

Reproducibility is weakened by an apparently missing/blank code repository link ("Code is available at" with no URL provided in the text) and no reported hyperparameter search protocol (e.g., the AdamW learning rate of 3 is unusual and unmotivated, with no ablation).

The comparison methodology (post-processing all methods, including baselines, by projecting to the exact-k combinatorial constraint) could obscure differences in the raw continuous solutions; it is unclear whether this post-processing is applied identically and fairly to all methods, and how much of the observed advantage of FW comes from this final projection step versus the continuous optimization itself.

The paper's presentation is dense with heavy notation and many deferred proofs to appendices, which, combined with the modest length of the main technical narrative, makes it hard to assess the depth of novelty without close reading of the appendices; some intuition for why the specific proof strategies were chosen (versus alternatives) is missing.

strengths: The paper provides a clean and rigorous theoretical improvement over prior work: it tightens the known sufficient condition for tightness of the diagonally-loaded relaxation of DkS from λ=2 (Barman) to λ=1, and importantly also establishes a matching lower-bound (via a novel extension of the Motzkin–Straus theorem) showing λ=1 is the minimum value guaranteeing tightness in the worst case. This closes an open gap explicitly identified in the related-work discussion.

The landscape analysis (Lemma 1 and Theorem 5) gives a clear, intuitive, and provable characterization of how increasing λ can only introduce (never remove) spurious local maxima, which nicely explains and motivates the empirically observed trade-off between λ=1 and larger values.

Two complementary projection-free algorithms are proposed (Frank–Wolfe and an explicit sigmoid/softmax-style parameterization for the more general Dn_k constraint), each with careful per-iteration complexity analysis; the parameterization for a sum-≤k constraint appears to be a genuinely new generalization of the softmax trick.

Empirical evaluation spans six real datasets ranging from thousands to millions of vertices/edges (including com-Orkut with >3M vertices and >117M edges), demonstrating that the FW-based method scales well and is competitive with or better than several recent baselines (L-ADMM, EXPP, LRBO, Greedy) in both density and runtime.

The paper is well organized, clearly distinguishes its formulation and relaxation diagram (Figure 1) from prior related approaches, and provides full proofs in the appendix for reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The parameter-selection study (Figures 2 and 3) validating λ=1 and the FW step-size choice is conducted only on the smallest dataset (Facebook, n=4,039); it is unclear whether the same qualitative behavior (fast convergence, integral solutions, avoidance of spurious optima) holds robustly on the larger, sparser graphs used in the main comparison.

Corollary 2's necessity argument for λ=1 is proven only for the regime k<ω using a further relaxation to the simplex-scaled set Δ^n_k; while sufficient to establish worst-case tightness of the bound, the practical relevance of this specific regime for real graphs (where ω is often small relative to interesting k, e.g., com-Youtube ω=17) is not discussed.

Several methods extensively discussed in Related Work (Hager et al., Sotirov's coordinate descent) are not included as empirical baselines, despite being close conceptual competitors (continuous relaxation + gradient-based optimization for DkS); their omission makes it harder to judge how much the proposed λ=1 diagonal loading and FW procedure improve over the most directly comparable prior gradient-based approaches.

Experimental protocol details are sparse: it is unclear whether results (density/runtime curves) are averaged over multiple runs/seeds (relevant since AdamW-parameterization is stochastic), and no variance/error bars are reported.
The paper text ends with an incomplete sentence ("Code is available at"), suggesting an unfinished or improperly redacted reproducibility statement/link.

The parameterization-based algorithm, despite being framed as a main contribution, is shown empirically to generally underperform the Frank–Wolfe method and incur higher computational cost, somewhat diminishing its practical value relative to the paper's stated contributions.
